Allergy Warning: Bee stings can cause severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) that are potentially fatal. Do not keep bees if you or household members have known severe bee allergies. Always carry epinephrine auto-injector if at risk. Ensure all people in household are trained in emergency response. Consider neighbor proximity—some areas restrict beekeeping due to public health concerns. Check local regulations before establishing apiary.

Overview

Beekeeping is both an agricultural practice and a symbiotic relationship with one of nature's most sophisticated organisms. A single honeybee colony provides honey, wax, pollination services, and medicinal compounds while requiring minimal resources in return. This guide covers everything from hive construction to harvest, bee biology to emergency preparedness.

Why Beekeeping Matters in Offline Scenarios: Honeybees pollinate 75% of global food crops. A single colony increases vegetable garden yield by 30-50% through pollination alone. In resource-scarce environments, a hive provides food, medicine, waterproofing, and light sources indefinitely.

Why Keep Bees

Honey

Honey is one of nature's most remarkable foods and preservatives. A single colony can produce 30-100 pounds of surplus honey annually, depending on region and climate. Honey contains approximately 64 calories per tablespoon and consists primarily of simple sugars (fructose, glucose) that provide immediate energy.

Preservation Properties

Honey's low moisture content (17-20%) creates an environment hostile to bacterial growth. Its high osmotic pressure literally dehydrates microorganisms. This makes honey one of the only foods that never spoils—archaeological honey from Egypt remains viable after 3,000+ years. For long-term storage, keep honey in sealed containers away from humidity. Honey may crystallize over time; gently warm to restore fluidity without damaging properties.

Honey stored in sealed glass jars will remain edible indefinitely. No refrigeration required. A single deep frame of honey (roughly 3-4 lbs) stores 25,000+ calories—valuable insurance against food scarcity.

Medicinal Uses

  • Wound healing: Raw honey's antibacterial enzymes produce hydrogen peroxide, accelerating tissue repair
  • Cough suppressant: Studies show raw honey rivals over-the-counter cough syrups
  • Digestive support: Honey contains prebiotics that feed beneficial gut bacteria
  • Anti-inflammatory: Reduces inflammation in throat and respiratory tract
  • Energy source: The glucose hits bloodstream immediately; fructose sustains longer

Beeswax

Produced by worker bees to build comb, beeswax is a waxy secretion from glands on their abdomen. One pound of beeswax requires 8-10 pounds of honey to produce. Unlike honey, beeswax can be melted, molded, and re-used indefinitely without degrading.

Beeswax Applications

  • Candles: Burns slower and cleaner than paraffin, produces bright flame, smells pleasant
  • Waterproofing: Rub on fabric, leather, rope—repels water and resists rot
  • Sealant: Seals jars, protects cut wood, creates weather-tight seals on containers
  • Furniture polish: Creates natural, food-safe finish on wood
  • Medicinal salves: Base for lip balm, healing creams, muscle rubs
  • Thread conditioning: Wax threads before sewing—reduces fraying, increases durability

Pollination Services

Even without harvest, a single colony provides tremendous value through pollination. Bees pollinate roughly 75% of global food crops. A healthy hive can visit 50,000-100,000 flowers in a single day. This translates directly to increased yields in nearby vegetable gardens, fruit trees, and crops. Many commercial agriculture operations keep bees specifically for pollination, often earning more from pollination contracts than honey sales.

Propolis

A sticky resin collected from tree buds, propolis serves as hive sealant and antibacterial agent. It contains potent compounds with antimicrobial, antifungal, and anti-inflammatory properties. Bees use it to seal cracks and prevent disease. Humans can harvest it by scraping propolis from the hive interior (wear gloves—it stains). Create a tincture by soaking in alcohol for 2-4 weeks, then straining. Use topically for wounds or internally in small doses for immune support.

Sustainability Note: One colony produces surplus honey/wax only after the bees have stored enough for their own survival. Always leave adequate stores for winter—never take all the honey or the colony will starve.

Bee Biology

Colony Structure

A honey bee colony is a superorganism—not merely a group of individual insects, but a collective entity with distributed cognition and remarkable communication.

The Queen

  • Only fertile female in the colony
  • Produces pheromones that regulate colony behavior and reproduction
  • Lays 1,500-2,000 eggs daily during peak season
  • Lives 2-5 years (compared to workers at 6 weeks)
  • Fed exclusively royal jelly throughout her life

Worker Bees

  • Sterile females performing all labor: nursing, building, foraging, defense
  • Live 6 weeks in summer, 4-6 months in winter
  • Progress through roles based on age: house bee (0-21 days), field bee (21-42 days)
  • Possess specialized structures: pollen baskets on hind legs, nectar stomach separate from digestive stomach
  • Perform approximately 12 jobs during their lifetime

Drone Bees

  • Males, produced from unfertilized eggs
  • Sole purpose: mate with virgin queens (rarely successful—only 0.1-1% mate)
  • Larger than workers, cannot sting, cannot feed themselves
  • Expelled from hive in fall to conserve winter resources
  • Live 40-60 days

Annual Cycle

Winter (December-February): Cluster in tight ball around queen, vibrating to generate heat (maintain 92-95°F in center). Consumption dramatically reduced; colony living off stored honey. No brood rearing. Workers live 4-6 months.

Early Spring (March-April): Queen begins laying, brood increases, population grows. Bees consume significant stores for energy to feed larvae. Critical period—inadequate stores = starvation. Assess hive weight.

Late Spring (May): Peak egg laying. Population explosion—hive grows from 10,000 to 40,000+ bees. Honey flow begins. Risk of swarming increases. Swarm cells visible when colony feels crowded.

Summer (June-August): Peak activity. Honey production. Multiple brood patterns. Continuous laying. Heat and humidity managed through fanning. Foragers work intensely. Drones present. Summer workers live only 5-6 weeks despite abundant food.

Early Fall (September): Brood rearing declines. Drones expelled. Colony shifts to preparation mode: reducing entrance, propolizing cracks, binding down equipment. Last generation of long-lived winter bees produced.

Late Fall (October-November): Brood nearly ceases. Males completely gone. Population stabilizes at 10,000-20,000 (minimum viable overwintering population). Final stores assessed. Insulation added. Entrance reduced.

Swarming Behavior

Swarming is the colony's reproductive strategy—when the hive feels overcrowded, it splits. A portion of the population (typically 30-50% plus the old queen) departs to establish a new colony. This is a critical window: swarms are docile (gorged with honey, seeking new home, not defensive) and vulnerable to capture.

Swarm signs: Multiple queen cells (large, peanut-shaped), reduced laying, bees clustering outside the hive, agitated behavior.

Prevention: Provide space (add supers before crowding), maintain young queens (old queens swarm more readily), manage hive configuration, split proactively.

Communication: The Waggle Dance

When a forager locates a nectar source, she returns to the hive and performs the waggle dance—a figure-eight pattern encoding direction and distance to the resource.

  • Direction: Angle relative to the sun (if 45° right of vertical, source is 45° right of sun)
  • Distance: Duration of waggle phase (longer = farther)
  • Quality: Vigor and duration of dance (rich source = longer dance)

Other bees observe the dance, memorize the pattern, and fly directly to the location—accurate to within meters at distances exceeding 3 miles. This is abstract symbolic communication, arguably more sophisticated than most animal language.

Understanding the waggle dance helps you appreciate bee intelligence and timing. Watch returning foragers during peak bloom—the intensity and duration of dances directly reflect nectar availability.

Climate & Environmental Requirements

Site Selection

Hive placement dramatically affects colony success. Bees need adequate forage, water, sunlight, and protection from elements.

Ideal Conditions

  • Sunlight: 6+ hours direct morning sun (warms cluster, reduces moisture)
  • Wind protection: Windbreaks on north/west sides (trees, fences)
  • Water access: Shallow dish, stream, or fountain within 100 feet
  • Forage: Diverse flowering plants within 1-mile radius (gardens, orchards, wildflowers)
  • Elevation: Low-wind areas; avoid exposed summits or frost pockets

Minimum Forage Requirement: Bees need roughly 2-3 acres of diverse flowering plants nearby to survive spring through fall. Urban/suburban gardens with diverse plantings work excellently.

Regional Climate Considerations

  • Temperate (4-season): Requires winter cluster preparation; plan for 25% winter loss
  • Tropical: Year-round management; moisture/disease control critical
  • Desert/Arid: Water source essential; shade required; compressed bloom windows
  • Coastal: Wind protection, salt-resistant finishes for equipment

Hive Placement

Location matters as much as local climate. Establish hives away from pedestrian traffic, roads, and neighbor disputes.

  • Distance from neighbors: Minimum 10 feet; 50+ feet preferred to reduce liability
  • Level ground: Sloped ground causes water pooling and robbing vulnerability
  • Stable surface: Concrete pad, level ground, or sturdy stand (prevents tipping)
  • Isolation: Separate hives by 6+ feet (reduces disease transmission)

Property Rights & Beekeeping Law: Local codes vary significantly. Some areas require permits, mandate setbacks from property lines, or prohibit beekeeping entirely. Research local regulations before establishing hives—otherwise you risk forced removal and neighbor conflict.

Hive Construction

Top-Bar Hive (Simplest Design)

The top-bar hive is ideal for offline scenarios—requires minimal tools, no precision lumber, and uses natural comb without frames. Bees build comb downward from wooden bars, mimicking natural tree cavity nesting. Construction is forgiving, and management is intuitive.

Top-Bar vs. Langstroth: Top-bar hives prioritize bee welfare and simplicity, while Langstroth maximizes yield and commercial compatibility. Choose based on goals: offline self-sufficiency favors top-bar; large-scale production favors Langstroth.

Advantages

  • Build with rough-sawn wood, no frame precision required
  • Lower cost than Langstroth setup
  • Bees construct comb naturally without commercial foundation
  • Easy hive inspection—lift bars individually
  • Reduced parasite pressure (bees manage comb ecology)
  • Works with captured swarms, no special equipment needed

Disadvantages

  • Honey extraction is crush-and-strain only (comb cannot be reused)
  • Slightly lower yields than Langstroth
  • Requires more frequent inspections to prevent burr comb

TYPICAL TOP-BAR HIVE DIMENSIONS (Kenya Hive Style) Internal dimensions: - Length: 47-49 inches - Width: 16 inches (provides 24-28 bars, 1.75" spacing) - Height: 10 inches (internal) Construction materials: - Lumber: 1" thick boards (pine or cedar), 12-16" wide - Top bars: 1.25" × 1.75" × 49" (one per bar, 24-28 total) - Wood thickness: 1.5" insulation value - Roof: sloped, extends 3-4" overhang all sides - Floor: solid wood, 1.5" inside, slight slope for drainage - Entrance: 1.5" × 4" at bottom, can be restricted with blocks - Cloth/burlap: for inner cover beneath roof Assembly: 1. Cut side boards 47-49" long 2. Cut front/back 16" with dovetail or lap joints for strength 3. Install cleats 7" up from bottom for top bars to rest on 4. Top bars rest on cleats, span width of hive 5. Roof slopes to rear; front extends lower 6. Install entrance reducers, drainage, ventilation

Langstroth Hive (Standard Commercial)

The Langstroth is the most widely used hive in commercial apiculture. It uses removable frames with foundation—bees build comb on the foundation, creating uniform, extractable combs. More complex to build but enables higher yields and easier management at scale.

Advantages

  • Frames are reusable year after year
  • Honey extraction with centrifugal force (extractor) = higher yields
  • Modular—add/remove boxes for seasonal needs
  • Compatible with commercial equipment and knowledge
  • Easier to assess queen laying patterns

Disadvantages

  • Requires precision lumber and woodworking
  • Foundation purchase needed (beeswax or plastic)
  • Higher initial cost
  • More intrusive inspections—remove entire frames

LANGSTROTH HIVE DIMENSIONS (10-frame standard) Deep box (brood chamber): - Internal: 16.25" × 19.875" × 9.625" - Wood thickness: 0.75" (exterior slightly larger) - Frame width: 1.625" (internal) - Spacing: center-to-center 1.375" - 10 frames per box, 9 deep combs typical Medium box (honey super): - Internal: 16.25" × 19.875" × 6.625" - Same frame dimensions as deep - Lighter—easier to lift when full of honey Shallow box: - Internal: 16.25" × 19.875" × 5.75" Frame components: - Top bar: 1.625" × 19.875" with pins/wedges - Side bars: 0.75" × 8.5" (deep) or 5.5" (medium) - Bottom bar: 1" × 19.875" - Foundation: 0.125" beeswax sheet (or plastic), embossed with hexagons

Skep Hive (Historical Woven Straw)

The skep is a domed hive woven from straw or wicker, used for centuries. While illegal in some countries (deemed inferior for bee welfare), understanding skep construction is valuable for offline preparedness. Bees build comb freely inside, no frames.

Construction Notes

  • Dome shape from coiled straw rope, bound with ash splints or hazel twigs
  • Entrance hole at bottom, 1.5-2" diameter
  • Roof/cover: straw roof or wooden lid with thatch
  • Base board underneath or set on straw/wood block
  • Interior smoother, less sharp surfaces than exterior
  • Typical diameter 16-18 inches, height 14-16 inches

Extraction challenge: Killing the colony or cutting comb (destructive). Modern view sees this as animal cruelty; however, in true collapse scenarios, knowledge of extraction may be necessary. Entire comb harvested as crush-and-strain.

Log/Tree Hive (Most Primitive)

A hollowed log section closed at both ends, entrance hole drilled at bottom. Bees build comb freely. Simplest form of beekeeping—minimal intervention required. Excellent for establishing feral populations.

Log Hive Construction

  • Log selection: 10-15" diameter, 24-36" length, hollow or carefully hollowed (dull chisel)
  • Interior: Smooth walls, remove loose bark. Rough interior actually preferred—bees attach comb better
  • Entrance: 1.5" hole drilled at bottom
  • Top: Wooden cap or bark piece, sealed with clay or mud
  • Bottom: Solid wood base, slight slope for drainage
  • Mounting: 4-8 feet up on post or tree (protection from predators)
  • Ventilation: Allow slight air exchange; seal well to prevent moisture

Advantages: Extremely low cost, completely offline, minimal maintenance. Disadvantages: Honey extraction requires killing bees or cutting comb, difficult to assess health, swarming uncontrolled.

Log hive extraction is destructive—the colony dies or must be relocated. Use log hives only in true resource-scarcity scenarios where other options unavailable, or establish them as "donation" colonies you harvest once annually.

Growth Stages & Colony Development

Eggs to Adult Timeline

Understanding bee development helps you assess colony health and predict population growth.

  • Egg: 3 days in cell (female develops on day 1; male on day 3)
  • Larva: 5-6 days (fed constantly by nurse bees; molts 5 times)
  • Pupae: 8-10 days (sealed in cell, metamorphosis occurs)
  • Total development time: Worker = 21 days; Drone = 24 days; Queen = 16 days

A healthy laying queen produces ~2,000 eggs daily during peak season. With 21-day development, a strong hive grows by roughly 5,000-7,000 bees per week in spring/early summer.

Population Cycle & Colony Strength

A strong colony reaches 40,000-60,000 bees in mid-summer. Winter population drops to 10,000-20,000 (minimum viable overwintering size). Understanding this cycle helps you:

  • Anticipate labor peaks (spring requires inspection; summer requires space management)
  • Assess colony health (weak spring = possible winter starvation)
  • Plan splits or requeening (best done when population >20,000)

Assessing Hive Strength

Strength Level Population Frame Coverage Honey Potential Winter Survival Risk
Weak 5,000-10,000 2-3 frames 0-5 lbs Very High
Fair 10,000-20,000 4-5 frames 5-20 lbs High
Good 20,000-35,000 6-8 frames 20-50 lbs Moderate
Excellent 35,000-60,000 9-10 frames 50-100+ lbs Low

Winter Survival Rule: Any hive with <5 frames of bees by September faces severe winter survival risk. Plan to feed, merge with stronger colony, or accept likely loss.

Getting Bees

Catching Swarms

A swarm is a free colony ready to establish itself. Swarms are docile, self-selected for desirable traits (successful foragers, good queens), and represent natural reproduction. Catching swarms is the cheapest, most rewarding method of acquiring bees.

Swarm Traps (Bait Hives)

  • Purpose: Attract homeless swarms during swarm season (May-June, sometimes July)
  • Design: Small box (5-10L) hung 12-25 feet high on pole or tree, entrance 1-1.5" diameter
  • Bait: Lemon grass oil (pheromone attractant) or used comb from previous bees
  • Interior: Rough wood, old comb, or straw for anchoring foundation
  • Placement: Edge of clearing, 100 yards from other hives, morning sun exposure
  • Timing: Set traps before peak swarm season; check daily during season

Swarm Capture Technique

  1. Observe swarm clustering (usually on branch, post, or structure)
  2. Wait 24 hours if possible—queen joins cluster after 2-4 hours, colony becomes "committed"
  3. Lay sheet beneath branch, shake limb so swarm falls onto sheet
  4. Scoop bees into hive box or cage, set entrance toward cluster
  5. Bees follow pheromone of queen into box—self-loading process
  6. Wait 2-3 hours; if most bees in, cover and transport
  7. Install in prepared hive with comb/foundation and entrance reducer

A hive box with a few old combs or straw inside will fill faster—bees cling to familiar scent. Mark the location where you captured the swarm; scout bees often retrace the flight path looking for stragglers.

Swarm Calling

In areas with many keepers, swarms often pass through. Local knowledge and communication increase success. Join local beekeeping associations; list yourself as available for swarm removal. Spread word among neighbors.

Splitting Existing Colonies

If you already have a hive or access to one, a split creates a new colony from resources of the old. Requires care to ensure both units survive.

Walk-Away Split Method

  1. In late spring when hive has excellent population and brood, prepare new hive box nearby
  2. Move original hive 4 feet to side
  3. Place new hive in original spot
  4. Transfer 4-5 combs with brood, pollen, nectar from original hive to new hive
  5. Include frame with eggs or young larva (for emergency queen cells)
  6. Return bees to new hive; field bees navigate to location, strengthen new colony
  7. Original hive at side gets all returning foragers daily—colony develops new queen
  8. Provide both units adequate stores; monitor for starvation

Risk: One or both hives may fail if not enough bees or food. Best done in strong flow, when forage abundant.

Finding & Catching Wild Colonies

In areas with established feral populations, wild colonies can be located and relocated.

Scout & Locate

  • Look for bee traffic during bloom—watch flowers, water sources
  • Follow bees in early morning or late afternoon (direct flight home)
  • Triangulate location; follow from multiple observation points
  • Likely homes: hollow trees, wall cavities, attics, rocky outcrops

Extraction & Relocation

  • Requires smoke, patience, protective gear
  • Extract comb with bees attached into boxes or cages
  • Locate and secure queen (critical—hive won't move without her)
  • Transport to new location; allow 24-48 hours orientation before opening
  • Success rate highly variable; strong reorientation risk

Ethics & Law: Confirm ownership of property before removing bees. Some jurisdictions require permits or prohibit relocation of wild bees. Document your actions. Offer compensation if on private land.

Seasonal Management

Spring (March-April)

First Inspection

  • On warm day (>55°F), open hive carefully on windless afternoon
  • Assess live/dead status: lift hive—feel weight (good sign if heavy)
  • Look for brood in multiple cells (indicates laying queen)
  • Check food stores—should have 3-4 frames of honey minimum
  • Remove dead bees, clean entrance, check for mold or disease
  • Replace old/moldy comb

Feeding & Nutrition

If hive light on stores, feed to prevent starvation. Sugar syrup (1:1 or 2:1 sugar:water) stimulates brood rearing. Continue until natural nectar flow arrives (fruit blossoms).

Spring Starvation Risk: Many colonies die in spring (March-April) despite surviving winter. This "spring dearth" occurs when bees consume winter stores during brood rearing but before plants bloom. Monitor weight and feed proactively.

Swarm Prevention

  • Checklist swarm signs: multiple queen cells, reduced laying, congestion
  • Provide space: add second box before crowding
  • Remove queen cells if prevention desired (or allow one to develop for controlled split)
  • Ensure young queen (2+ year old queens swarm more readily)

Summer (May-August)

Honey Supers

  • Add honey supers (lighter boxes) before main flow (local indicator: acacia blooms, wildflowers dense)
  • Place across top of brood chamber with excluder (optional but recommended—prevents queen in super)
  • Add second super if first becomes 2/3 full
  • Watch for filling speed; harvest partially if colony crowded

Monitoring & Maintenance

  • Weekly visual inspection: entrance activity, flight pattern, population presence
  • Monthly (or bi-weekly) detailed inspection if time allows
  • Ensure water source available (shallow dish, pebbles, or bee water feeder)
  • Manage grass/vegetation—maintain clear area around hive
  • Monitor for obvious disease or aggressive behavior

Management Decisions

  • Allow swarms or conduct controlled split (depends on goals)
  • Manage drone comb if varroa mites present (remove drone brood comb to break mite cycle)
  • Assess nectar/pollen availability; supplemental feeding if drought

Fall (September-October)

Honey Harvest

  • Harvest supers when 80%+ capped (ready for extraction)
  • Use crush-and-strain method (no extractor needed—see Honey Harvest section)
  • Remove supers before killing frost—bees need time to cluster

Winterization

  • Assess stores: Brood chamber must contain 40-60 pounds of honey (6-8 frames for top-bar, varies by hive type)
  • Reduce entrance: Install entrance reducer (1/4" hole) to minimize heat loss and prevent robbing
  • Add insulation: Wrap hive in tar paper or woodchip insulation; slope roof for drainage
  • Medication: Treat for varroa mites if population present (see Bee Health section)
  • Monitor brood: Confirm queen laid last autumn brood (long-lived winter bees essential)

Late Fall Feeding

If stores inadequate, feed heavy syrup (2:1 sugar:water) or fondant (powdered sugar + honey) to build winter stores. Bees must process and store before cluster-up. Feed in September-early October; stop before hard freeze.

Winter (November-February)

Monitoring

  • Minimal intervention—disturbance breaks cluster and kills bees
  • Visual inspection only: check entrance for dead bees (sign of disease) or moisture
  • Weigh hive monthly (can lift back end—should feel heavy) or estimate stores
  • Clear entrance snow/ice but don't disturb

Insulation & Ventilation Balance

  • Hive must retain heat (insulation) but manage moisture (ventilation)
  • Top entrance/vent reduces moisture accumulation
  • Sloped roof diverts moisture away from cluster
  • Adequate insulation on sides and roof

Emergency Feeding

If hive light on stores (can assess by weight), provide emergency food without opening hive. Methods: place candy board (fondant/sugar patty) on top bars, or medicated sugar water drip feeders accessible from outside.

Water & Nutrient Management

Water Requirements

Bees need clean water year-round—for drinking, brood rearing, and colony cooling (in summer, they splash water on comb to reduce temperature). A single colony consumes 15-20 gallons of water weekly during heavy nectar flow.

Water Source Establishment

  • Shallow dish: Saucer, bird bath, or container with pebbles/cork floating in water (prevents bees from drowning)
  • Proximity: Within 100 feet of hive (preferred) or up to 1 mile radius
  • Freshness: Change water every 2-3 days to prevent mosquito breeding and algae growth
  • Insulation: In cold climates, provide heated water (slightly warm) in late winter when ice forms

Bees prefer shallow water with landing pads. A ceramic saucer with rocks or moss inside works excellently—bees land on solid surface, drink at water level without falling in.

Nutrition: Nectar, Pollen & Supplements

Nectar provides carbohydrates (honey production); pollen provides protein, fats, and minerals. A healthy hive requires both.

  • Pollen sources: Diverse flowering plants (fruit blossoms, wildflowers, legumes, native shrubs)
  • Nectar flows: Timed blooms throughout season (spring: fruit trees; summer: wildflowers/alfalfa; fall: asters/goldenrod)
  • Dearth periods: Spring (before bloom) and mid-summer (between flows) require supplemental feeding

Emergency Feeding

When forage unavailable (spring starvation, drought, late winter), provide:

  • Sugar syrup: 1:1 (spring) or 2:1 (fall/winter) sugar:water; provide in top feeder or frame feeder (inside hive, prevents robbing)
  • Fondant/candy board: Powdered sugar + honey mixture molded into patty; place on top bars above cluster (accessible without breaking cluster)
  • Quantity: Estimate 10-20 lbs. syrup for spring; 20-40 lbs. for fall/winter

Feeding Timing: Stop feeding by early September (fall) to prevent fermentation and ensure proper ripening. Spring feeding (March-April) critical to prevent starvation during brood rearing.

Pest & Disease Management

Varroa Destructor Mites

The single greatest threat to managed honeybees. Varroa mites are parasites that feed on hemolymph (bee blood), weakening individual bees and transmitting viruses. An untreated mite population doubles every 4-6 weeks. High mite loads lead to colony collapse, typically in fall/winter.

Identification

  • Appearance: Reddish-brown, flat, oval mites (1-2mm), visible to naked eye on bees
  • Location: Found on bee bodies and in brood cells (especially drone cells)
  • Signs of infestation: Twisted wings (deformed wing virus), spotty brood, crawling bees

Monitoring Mite Load

  • Sugar roll: Place 300 bees in jar, add powdered sugar, roll jar gently—mites stick to sugar, fall into bottom. Count mites: <5 = acceptable, 5-10 = monitor, >10 = treat immediately
  • Sticky board: Place board under screen hive floor (bees above screen). Mites fall through. Count over 24 hours; <3/day acceptable, >10/day = serious infestation
  • Visual inspection: Open hive; look for mites on bees and in capped brood

Natural/Non-Chemical Treatments

Powdered Sugar Dusting - Safest method, no toxins, repeatable

  • Mix 1 pound powdered sugar with hive frames/bees (dust on bees during inspection)
  • Mites lose grip and fall; bees groom sugar off, resume normal behavior
  • Must repeat every 5-7 days for 4-6 weeks (during brood-free period, most effective)
  • Treatment rate: dust entire exposed brood frame area

Drone Comb Removal - Integrated pest management

  • Varroa prefer drone (male) brood 15:1 over worker brood
  • Encourage drone comb production by using larger-cell foundation or cutting comb to 6mm cells
  • When drone comb capped, cut out and remove (freeze or discard); new comb grows, mites concentrated in it
  • Repeat monthly during brood season—removes 30-40% mite population

Screened Bottom Board - Passive control

  • Install screen at hive bottom (mites naturally fall and can't climb back)
  • Must be unobstructed; sticky board below catches fallen mites
  • Provides airflow (ventilation benefit) and passive mite reduction

Hive Replacement - Long-term strategy

  • Replace 1-2 combs annually (older comb contains more mites/pathogens)
  • Requeen every 1-2 years with young, vigorous queens
  • Maintain small-cell foundation (5.4mm vs. standard 5.8mm) if possible—bees cap brood faster, reducing mite reproduction

American Foulbrood (AFB)

Bacterial disease (Paenibacillus larvae) causing larvae death, severe for beekeeping. Spores extremely persistent—can survive >40 years in honey.

Symptoms

  • Sunken, dark capped brood
  • Ropy slime strands when comb opened (characteristic "ropey" appearance)
  • Smell: sour, sickly-sweet odor
  • Scattered dead pupae, not mass brood death

Management

  • Confirm diagnosis: Only antibiotic (Terramycin/oxytetracycline) is effective treatment
  • If no chemicals available: Destroy affected combs, possibly entire hive (most reliable approach)
  • Prevention: Never transfer combs between hives without confirmation of health; practice sanitation
  • Legal note: Many regions require reporting and may mandate destruction of affected colonies

American Foulbrood is extremely contagious. Spores persist >40 years; equipment, tools, even beekeeper clothing can spread disease. If AFB confirmed, sterilize or destroy all equipment used with affected hive. This is not optional—AFB kills feral colonies and spreads rapidly.

Combined Health Management Table

American Foulbrood Ropy appearance, sunken capped brood, smell Critical (highly contagious) Destruction of affected combs/hive only option without antibiotics
European Foulbrood Unsealed brood, yellow-brown larvae, smell Moderate (often self-resolves) Remove affected combs, improve hive conditions, strong colony management
Small Hive Beetles Larval tunnels in comb, larvae visible Moderate (warm climates) Freezing combs, strong colonies, petroleum jelly entrance

European Foulbrood (EFB)

Less severe than AFB; often resolves without treatment if hive strong. Caused by various Melissococcus bacteria.

Symptoms

  • Unsealed (uncapped) brood with dead larvae
  • Yellow-brown discoloration of larva
  • Mild sour smell (less intense than AFB)
  • Scattered pattern, not systematic

Treatment

  • Often self-limiting in strong colonies (bees uncap and remove diseased larvae)
  • Improve hive conditions: ensure adequate food, reduce crowding, maintain young queen
  • Remove affected combs if severe
  • Antibiotics (oxytetracycline) effective if chemical treatment available

Nosema

Fungal infection (Nosema ceranae) of gut lining. Weakens winter survival; adult bees become dysenteric. Diagnosis requires microscope.

  • Prevention: Maintain young, healthy queen; ensure adequate stores; good hive sanitation
  • Treatment: No cure; supportive care—ensure warm shelter, adequate food, ventilation
  • Mitigation: Replace infected combs; disinfect equipment if moving between hives

Small Hive Beetles

A pest (Aethina tumida) in warm climates. Larvae tunnel through comb, contaminating honey with larvae and feces.

Control Methods

  • Maintain strong colonies: Strong hives suppress beetle populations
  • Remove and freeze combs: If beetles present, place comb in freezer (below 50°F) overnight to kill larvae
  • Reduce hive volume: Remove empty comb, keeping hive space small—bees control beetles better in compact space
  • Entrance reducers: Restrict entrance to reduce beetle escape
  • Petroleum jelly/oil: Smear around hive entrance—beetles get stuck trying to enter/exit

General Health Maintenance

PracticeBenefitFrequency
Hive inspection for brood patternsDetect disease early, assess queen layingMonthly during season
Replace old comb (3-4 year rotation)Reduce pathogen/toxin buildup1-2 frames annually
Requeen every 1-2 yearsMaintain genetics, vigor, pheromone healthAnnually or biennially
Ensure adequate stores (winter)Prevent starvation, reduce winter stressLate summer assessment
Maintain clean, dry hivesPrevent fungal/moisture problemsOngoing

When to Accept Loss: In offline/collapse scenarios, some losses are inevitable. Focus on preventing disease spread to other colonies. A dead hive teaches valuable lessons and its comb/products can still be rendered for value.

Offline Health Summary: Without modern medicines, prevent disease through: strong colony management, regular comb replacement (every 3-4 years), consistent mite monitoring (monthly sugar rolls), and rapid isolation/destruction of infected hives before disease spreads.

Harvest & Storage

Honey Harvest Timing & Assessment

Honey is ready when capped (sealed with beeswax) and moisture content below 20%. Capped honey indicates bees believe it's shelf-stable and protected. Harvest too early and honey may ferment; too late and you'll lose the crop to early winter.

Readiness Assessment

  • Visual: At least 70-80% of comb surface capped with white wax
  • Timing: Late summer/early fall, before first hard frost
  • Weight: Frames with honey feel substantially heavier than empty frames
  • Smell: Ripe honey has fragrant, strong aroma
  • Taste: Take small sample on stick—should be thick, not runny

Extraction Methods

The crush-and-strain method is ideal for offline scenarios (no extractor needed) and works excellently with top-bar hives.

For Langstroth hives, consider building a simple hand-crank extractor from wood and metal screen, or alternate between crush-and-strain and frame reuse (frames without combs can be drawn again next season).

Beeswax Harvesting & Processing

Save all cappings (removed when uncapping honey), old comb, and burr comb. One pound of rendered beeswax has significant trade value or personal utility.

Rendering Methods

Solar Wax Melter (Simplest): Build wooden box (24"×24"×12" deep), line with plastic, slant glass sheet at 30-45° angle, paint interior black. Place comb scraps inside; wax melts and collects below. Multiple filterings remove debris.

Double-Boiler (Any Weather): Heat water gently (<180°F), place comb/cappings in top pot, allow wax to melt gradually. Pour through cheesecloth into cold water; wax hardens into disk. Re-melt multiple times for purity.

Beeswax Products: Rendered wax becomes candles (dipped or molded), waterproofing (fabric, rope, wood), salves, and furniture polish. Three renderings produce nearly white, premium-grade wax.

Products & Uses

Mead (Honey Wine)

Mead is fermented honey—the oldest known alcoholic beverage (older than beer or wine). Honey fermented with water and wild or cultured yeast produces a distinctive, age-worthy drink.

Simple Mead Recipe

  • Ingredients: 3-5 pounds honey per gallon of water (adjusts final ABV); no other ingredients required (wild fermentation) or add yeast (ale, champagne, or mead yeast)
  • Preparation: Mix honey and water (warm gently to dissolve if needed); cool to room temperature
  • Fermentation: Add yeast (if using) or leave covered in cloth for wild fermentation. Ferment in glass carboy with airlock 2-4 months (until bubble rate slows dramatically)
  • Bottling: Siphon into bottles; cap and age 6+ months (improves significantly with age)
  • Final ABV: Typical range 10-16% (higher honey = higher alcohol)

Mead improves dramatically with age (1-5+ years). A batch started today stores indefinitely in sealed bottles, providing shelf-stable alcohol and calories for survival scenarios.

Mead Variations

  • Melomel: Mead with fruit (berries, apples, stone fruit)
  • Metheglin: Mead with herbs/spices (ginger, clove, cinnamon—medieval style)
  • Cyser: Mead with apple juice
  • Pyment: Mead with grape juice

Propolis Tincture

Propolis (bee glue) has powerful antimicrobial and wound-healing properties. A simple tincture extracts these compounds into alcohol.

Preparation

  1. Collect propolis by scraping hive interior (gloves recommended—stains permanently)
  2. Place in glass jar; cover with high-proof alcohol (80+ proof vodka minimum, 190-proof grain alcohol ideal)
  3. Seal and store in cool, dark place for 2-4 weeks
  4. Strain through cheesecloth; discard solids
  5. Store tincture in amber bottles away from light

Uses

  • Topical wound treatment: apply 1-2 drops to cuts, abrasions; repeat 2-3× daily
  • Sore throat: gargle with few drops in water (don't swallow)
  • Immune support: 5-10 drops daily in tea or water (internal use)
  • Antifungal: apply to fungal infections

Beeswax Candles

Described earlier under Beeswax Processing; note the premium properties: clean burn, pleasant scent, long-lasting.

Furniture Polish & Wood Care

Beeswax Wood Polish

  • Recipe: Mix 1 part melted beeswax with 2-3 parts linseed oil
  • Application: Rub onto wood with cloth; polish with clean cloth
  • Result: Natural sheen, food-safe, moisture-resistant

Leather Conditioner

  • Beeswax mixed with lanolin (or tallow) conditions leather
  • Apply sparingly to boots, saddles, belts
  • Waterproofs while maintaining flexibility

Thread Conditioning

A simple but valuable use: pull sewing thread through beeswax before stitching. The wax prevents fraying, increases thread strength, and makes hand-sewing smoother. Particularly valuable for repairs in field/survival situations.

Honey as Wound Dressing

Medical research has validated traditional use: honey (especially raw, with pollen intact) accelerates wound healing.

Mechanism

  • Osmotic effect: High sugar concentration draws moisture from wound, reducing bacterial proliferation
  • Hydrogen peroxide: Enzymes in honey (glucose oxidase) produce hydrogen peroxide, cleaning the wound
  • Anti-inflammatory: Reduces inflammation and promotes tissue regeneration
  • Antibacterial compounds: Methylglyoxal and other components kill bacteria directly

Application

  • Clean wound gently with water
  • Apply layer of raw honey directly to wound
  • Cover with clean bandage (honey is messy)
  • Change dressing and reapply honey daily until healed
  • Particularly effective for burns, cuts, abrasions, and slow-healing sores

Note: Do not use for deep infections or puncture wounds where infection risk is high—professional medical care needed in those cases.

Safety

Protective Equipment from Scratch

Veil (From Window Screen)

  • Materials: Window screen (metal preferred for durability), elastic or cord, brim material (hat or stiffener)
  • Construction: Sew screen to elastic band; attach band to stiff brim (coat hanger works); create drawstring at bottom to tighten around jacket collar
  • Design: Full-face veil extends 18-24" below hat; face stays 2-3" away from screen to prevent stinging
  • Benefit: Bees confuse screen as part of vegetation; won't sting through mesh

Gloves (Makeshift)

  • Commercial gloves: Leather work gloves or beekeeping gauntlets (preferred)
  • Emergency: Wrap hands in leather or fabric; secure at wrist with elastic or cord
  • Note: Gloves reduce dexterity; many experienced beekeepers go bare-handed using calmness and speed

Suit/Clothing

  • Light-colored clothing: Bees are less aggressive toward light colors
  • Long sleeves and pants: Tuck pants into socks or boots; cover all skin
  • Avoid dark/fuzzy materials: Resemble predators (bears)
  • Anchor clothing: Tighten cuffs and collar so bees can't crawl in

Smoker Construction

A smoker masks alarm pheromones, calming bees. Smoke makes bees think hive is in danger, triggering feeding rather than aggression.

DIY Smoker

  • Container: Metal can (3.5-4" diameter, 4-5" tall—food can or paint can)
  • Draft tube: Metal pipe or drilled rod running through bottom (creates oxygen flow)
  • Bellows: Improvised from leather or fabric (tied to pipe or separate)
  • Fuel: Dried grass, straw, wood chips, cardboard—material that smolders (not burns)
  • Construction: Drill holes around can bottom for air intake; pipe exits through top; grate inside holds fuel

Using Smoke Safely

  • Light smoker 5-10 minutes before work; let fuel catch
  • Use gentle puffs; excessive smoke stresses bees and degrades honey flavor
  • Work with bee flight direction (smoke bees in one direction, work from opposite side)
  • Smoke entrance before opening hive (prevents bees rushing out)
  • Keep smoker away from hive when not actively calming

Sting Treatment

Immediate Care

  • Remove stinger: Scrape stinger off with flat edge (fingernail, knife)—avoid pinching (squeezes toxin in)
  • Clean area: Wash with soap and water to prevent infection
  • Ice: Apply ice pack 15-20 minutes to reduce swelling and pain
  • Elevation: Raise affected limb above heart if possible
  • Alkaline treatment: Baking soda paste or honey application (honey's antibacterial also reduces reaction)

Pain Management

  • Over-the-counter antihistamine (if available) reduces itching/swelling
  • Topical hydrocortisone cream
  • Pain relief: acetaminophen or ibuprofen

Infection Prevention

  • Resist scratching (itching worse if scratched)
  • Watch for spreading redness, increasing swelling, warmth (signs of infection)
  • Apply honey topically (antibacterial) if infected or slow-healing

Anaphylaxis Warning

A small percentage of humans develop severe allergic reactions to bee venom. Anaphylaxis is life-threatening and requires immediate medical intervention.

Warning Signs

  • Rapid swelling beyond sting area (face, throat, lips)
  • Difficulty breathing or wheezing
  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
  • Dizziness or loss of consciousness
  • Rapid or irregular heartbeat

Response

  • If known allergic: Carry epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen); use immediately if symptoms develop
  • Call emergency services: Do not delay seeking medical care
  • If unknown allergy: Stop beekeeping immediately if mild anaphylaxis signs (significant swelling beyond sting); avoid bee exposure

Critical: Anyone with known severe bee allergy should NOT keep bees. The risk of exposure during hive work is unacceptably high. Anaphylaxis can develop within minutes; in offline scenarios, medical response severely limited.

Climate Adaptations & Regional Variations

Tropical/Subtropical Regions

In warm climates (>75°F year-round), beekeeping dynamics differ significantly from temperate zones.

Management Differences

  • Year-round brood rearing: Queens lay continuously; no winter cluster period
  • Moisture management critical: High humidity promotes mold and fungal disease
  • Swarm prevention challenging: Lack of resource scarcity reduces natural population regulation
  • Shorter lifespan: Heat stress reduces worker lifespan (3-4 weeks instead of 6)

In tropical regions, maintain smaller colonies (10,000-15,000 bees) to reduce overheating stress. Ensure abundant water sources; screened ventilation on sides helps air circulation.

Regional Advantages

  • Longer forage season (may produce 2-3 flows annually)
  • Multiple queens possible in some hot climates (rare, unusual but documented in stingless bee species)
  • Less disease pressure from foulbrood (not well-adapted to sustained heat)

Temperate Regions (4-Season Climate)

Standard temperate region (northern US, Europe, Canada) shows the annual cycle described in Bee Biology.

Climate-Specific Challenges

  • Spring dearth: Gap between winter stores and spring bloom (see info-box earlier)
  • Summer heat stress: Hives >95°F reduce laying, increase mortality
  • Fall preparation critical: 6-8 weeks to build winter stores
  • Winter losses inevitable: 10-20% colony loss typical even with good management

Temperate Zone Beekeeping Rule: Assume 25% winter loss when planning. If keeping 4 hives, expect 1 to perish. Start with strong colony or split existing hive to have backup.

Desert/Arid Regions

Low rainfall, extreme temperature swings, scattered bloom times.

Adaptations

  • Water source essential: Without bees die of thirst before starvation
  • Shaded hive placement: Morning sun for warmth; afternoon shade critical
  • Dearth planning: Identify annual bloom windows (mesquite, creosote, wildflowers)
  • Winter mild but water-scarce: No cold cluster needed; dehydration risk instead

Desert Beekeeping Challenge: Extended dearths (6+ months between blooms) require careful feeding and storing. Plan to provide 60-80 lbs. honey stores in arid regions, more than temperate zones.

Coastal/Maritime Regions

Salt spray, strong winds, cool summers.

Adjustments

  • Wind protection: Build windbreaks; elevated hives catch wind
  • Salt damage: Paint hive equipment with marine-grade finish
  • Short season: Late spring bloom, early fall finish—compressed production window
  • Fog/cool impacts: Longer foraging windows (bees active in cool, overcast weather)

Yield Expectations & Production Reality

Realistic First-Year Yields

A package of bees (purchased colony starter) or first swarm produces little surplus honey the first season because:

  1. Bees must draw comb (8-10 weeks labor-intensive)
  2. Population takes time to build (4-6 weeks to double)
  3. Brood rearing consumes nectar (eggs → larvae → pupae costs calories)
  4. Only after population >30,000 and comb ready does real surplus accumulate

Typical first-year outcome: 0-10 pounds surplus (or zero if weak season). Do not expect harvest year one.

Second & Subsequent Year Yields

  • Top-bar hive: 20-50 pounds surplus annually (depends on region, weather, beekeeper skill)
  • Langstroth hive: 50-100+ pounds surplus (up to 200 in exceptional seasons)
  • Variables: Forage availability, winter losses, mite pressure, disease, queen quality

Rather than chasing high yields, aim for 30-40 pounds annually while maintaining strong, healthy colonies. Aggressive harvest practices lead to winter starvation and colony losses.

Non-Honey Products Income

Many sidestream products add value without compromising colony health:

  • Pollination contracts: $40-60 per hive per season (almond orchards, farms)
  • Nuc/split sales: $75-150 per starter hive
  • Queens: $20-50 each (for breeders)
  • Pollen patties/equipment: Niche but profitable
  • Beeswax products: Candles, salves (higher margin per pound than honey)

Troubleshooting

Absconding

Colony abandons hive completely—bees fly away, leaving eggs/brood to perish. Indicates severe problem or unsuitable hive conditions.

Common Causes

  • Insufficient food: Starvation fear triggers departure
  • Poor ventilation: Excessive moisture, mold, CO₂ buildup
  • Queen failure: Dead or failing queen causes colony disintegration
  • Extreme pest pressure: High mite load, beetles, or wax moths
  • Hive damage: Broken comb, rodent damage, structural failure
  • Wrong hive location: Moved after bees oriented to original spot; they return to original location

Prevention & Recovery

  • Ensure adequate food stores before and during season
  • Maintain proper ventilation and moisture management
  • Monitor queen laying patterns; requeen if decline evident
  • Control pests aggressively
  • Never relocate established hives; if necessary, move >2 miles or less than 3 feet
  • If absconded, clean hive thoroughly, repair damage, and restock with new swarm/package

Aggressive Colonies

Some colonies develop aggressive temperament—sting readily, pursue, exhibit high-strung behavior. Partially genetic, partially environmental.

Causes & Solutions

  • Genetics: Some hives bred for aggression (or poor genetics). Solution: requeen with calm genetics
  • Older queen: 3+ year old queens produce aggressive daughters. Solution: replace with young queen annually
  • Excessive pest pressure: Defensive behavior increases with mites/disease. Solution: treat pests, improve health
  • Poor feed timing: Robbing and starvation stress increase aggression. Solution: manage feeding properly, ensure stores
  • Excessive handling: Repeated, rough inspections increase defensiveness. Solution: minimize hive visits, work gently

Immediate Management

  • Work in cool weather (morning, overcast) when bees less active
  • Use heavy smoke; bees stay docile when focusing on self-preservation
  • Minimize hive opening; work quickly and intentionally
  • Consider requeening if aggression severe and other factors ruled out
  • In extreme cases, destroy colony if danger to yourself or neighbors

Queen Failure

Queen stops laying or dies, colony cannot reproduce. Without queen, colony collapses within weeks (no brood replacement).

Symptoms

  • Absence of eggs/young brood (larvae still present if recent failure)
  • Worker bees laying eggs (appear scattered, multiple per cell, laid on sides)
  • Reduced population (no new brood, colony not replacing losses)
  • Nervous, erratic colony behavior

Recovery

  • Emergency queen cell: If hive has eggs/young larvae, bees will build emergency queen cells (rare in feral queens)
  • Requeen with purchased queen: Place new queen in cage with escort bees; introduce over 3-5 days (allows hive to accept new pheromone profile)
  • Combine with another hive: If queenless colony weak, merge with strong colony (newspaper method—separate colonies by newspaper, gradually tear away so bees acclimate to each other)
  • Start over: If no replacement available, clean hive and restock with new swarm/package

Robbing Behavior

Foragers from one colony enter another and steal honey. Leads to fights, colony weakness, potential disease transmission.

Prevention

  • Reduce entrance: Use entrance reducers (limit bees able to defend)
  • Feed inside hive: Use internal feeders rather than outside feeders (prevent attracting robber bees)
  • Manage equal strength: Avoid weak hives near strong ones (screen weak hives or combine)
  • Minimize nectar shortage: Supplement during dearth (lack of natural forage)
  • Isolate hives: Space several feet apart; vary hive appearances (colors, configurations)

Intervention

  • If robbing observed, shut down entrance completely for 2-3 days (bees stop orienting to that location)
  • Then open entrance slowly with reducer
  • Move affected hive if possible (breaks foraging orientation)
  • Strengthen weak hive by giving brood frames from strong colony

Winter Survival Issues

Starvation

  • Prevention: Ensure 40-60 pounds honey in brood chamber before winter
  • Assessment: Weigh hive monthly or judge by feel (lift back edge—should feel heavy)
  • Emergency feeding: Provide fondant or sugar patties if stores insufficient (cannot open hive mid-winter without breaking cluster and causing deaths)

Excessive Moisture

  • Cause: Bees exhale moisture when clustered; hive must have ventilation
  • Prevention: Upper entrance/vent allows moist air to escape
  • Sloped roof: Directs condensation away from cluster
  • Absorbent material: Cloth or burlap above cluster absorbs moisture before dripping back

Dysentery/Disease

  • Symptom: Brown staining on hive exterior, musty smell
  • Cause: Usually associated with poor sanitation, nosema, or inadequate cleansing flights
  • Prevention: Ensure dry hive, ventilation, regular comb replacement
  • Treatment: Supportive only; replace combs if available, ensure clean entrance

Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them

Beginner Errors

Overconfidence in first year: New beekeepers often expect large honey crops year one. Colonies need 2-3 years to reach productive capacity. Accept minimal yields; focus on hive health instead.

Set a goal of "no winter losses" for your first two years instead of "50 lbs. honey." This mindset prevents aggressive harvest that kills colonies.

Excessive hive inspections: Every opening breaks cluster, disturbs brood patterns, and disrupts colony cohesion. Limit inspections to 2-3 times per season after initial setup.

Ignoring mite monitoring: Many beekeepers don't check mite loads until too late. Commit to monthly sugar roll or sticky board checks June–September.

Poor winter preparation: Assessing stores "by eye" is inaccurate. Weigh hive or test with hand—should feel heavy. Underfed hives starve in February/March when outdoor inspection impossible.

Seasonal Mistakes

Spring: Delaying first inspection until weather "perfect"—colonies can starve mid-March. Inspect by early April even if cool.

Summer: Leaving supers on too late (traps bees above excluder, forces crowding). Remove supers by mid-September regardless of cap %.

Fall: Harvesting too aggressively, leaving <40 lbs. stores. A good rule: if uncertain, leave it.

Winter: Opening hive to "check on bees"—this breaks cluster and kills dozens. Leave hives closed November–February; only assess weight/entrance.

Equipment Mistakes

  • Using plastic instead of woodenware: Plastic hives degrade in UV; harder for bees to attach wax. Wooden hives outlast plastic by decades.
  • Inadequate ventilation: Hives without upper entrance or ventilation develop moisture problems. Condensation drips on cluster, killing bees.
  • Poor drainage: Sloped floors essential; standing water inside hive = mold, fungal disease.

Quick Reference: Beekeeping at a Glance

Phase Timeline Key Action Success Indicator Common Failure
Setup 6-8 weeks before season Build/acquire hive; source bees (swarm, package, split) Hive installed by early spring Starting too late; no backup plan if bees fail
Spring Buildup March–May Feed if needed; monitor brood; prevent swarming Population grows 5,000+ bees/week; no starvation Starvation from delayed feeding; uncontrolled swarming
Summer Production June–August Add supers; minimal inspection; manage pests Supers filling; healthy brood patterns; low mite count Crowding leads to poor health; mites explode unchecked
Fall Harvest September–early October Harvest honey; assess stores; treat mites; begin insulation 40–60 lbs. honey in brood chamber; mite count <10 Insufficient stores; late harvest traps bees without time to cluster
Winter Survival November–February Minimize disturbance; monitor weight; provide emergency feed if needed Tight cluster; heavy hive; clean entrance; no disease Starvation from underestimated consumption; excessive moisture death

Single Most Important Rule: Ensure adequate food stores (40–60 lbs. in brood chamber before winter). This prevents 80% of colony failures. All other management is secondary to this.
